name: Tulsi
question_title: How do you care for a tulsi plant in the UAE?
quick_answer: Tulsi plant care in the UAE comes down to sun and drainage. Give holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum) at least six hours of direct sun a day, keep the soil moist but never waterlogged, and cut the stem tips to keep it bushy. In the UAE summer, give the pot afternoon shade and test the soil more often, because small pots dry out fast.

quick_facts.label: Light
quick_facts.value: Full sun: six or more hours of direct sun a day (NC State Extension). Afternoon shade from May to September.

quick_facts.label: Water
quick_facts.value: Keep the soil moist but never waterlogged. Feel the top of the soil before you water.

quick_facts.label: Soil
quick_facts.value: Well-drained potting mix in a pot with a drainage hole. Holy basil does poorly in waterlogged soil.

quick_facts.label: Temperature
quick_facts.value: Likes heat. Basil does not tolerate cold and is damaged by frost (Iowa State Extension): protect it on cold inland nights.

quick_facts.label: Best place in the UAE
quick_facts.value: A sunny balcony, terrace or garden. Indoors only at the sunniest window.

quick_facts.label: Size
quick_facts.value: Grows fast, to about 90 cm (3 ft) (NC State Extension).

quick_facts.label: Life span
quick_facts.value: Annual or short-lived perennial. It seeds itself easily.

quick_facts.label: Flowers
quick_facts.value: Spikes of tiny white, pale pink or lavender flowers.

quick_facts.label: Pets
quick_facts.value: No pet-safety listing exists for holy basil. The ASPCA lists sweet basil, a different species, as non-toxic to cats and dogs.

good_if: You have a balcony, terrace, garden or window that gets direct sun for most of the day.
You want a tulsi plant for home worship, or to give as a gift.
You want a fast-growing, fragrant herb that you can cut again and again.
You can check the soil often in summer, when pots dry out quickly.
think_twice: Your only spot is an AC room with no direct sun: tulsi gets thin and leggy there.
You travel often in summer and nobody can water: a small pot in the sun dries out fast.
You want a plant that keeps its shape for many years: tulsi is an annual or short-lived perennial.

care_sections.heading: How much sun does a tulsi plant need?
paragraphs: A tulsi plant needs full sun, which NC State Extension defines as six or more hours of direct sunlight a day. On a sunny UAE balcony, terrace or garden, holy basil grows fast and stays bushy. In less sun, tulsi growth gets weak and spindly and the leaves get pale, which the RHS lists as signs of too little light.

Tulsi likes heat (UT Gardens: hot weather does not bother it), but UAE summer sun on a balcony is intense, and small pots heat up and dry out fast. From May to September, put the tulsi pot where it gets morning sun and shade in the afternoon, and test the soil more often.

care_sections.heading: How often should you water a tulsi plant in the UAE?
paragraphs: Water a tulsi plant when the top of the soil feels dry, not on a fixed schedule. NC State Extension says holy basil prefers moist, well-drained soil and does poorly in waterlogged soil, so the aim is soil that is damp but never soggy. To test, push a finger into the soil up to the first knuckle: if it feels dry, water; if it feels damp, wait and test again later.

How fast tulsi soil dries depends on the pot and the weather. Small pots, terracotta pots, full sun, hot wind and the summer months dry the soil fastest, so an outdoor tulsi in summer needs water much more often than in winter. Large plastic pots, shade, coastal humidity and the cooler months keep the soil damp for longer.

When you water tulsi, water the soil at the base of the plant until water runs out of the drainage hole, then empty the saucer. Iowa State Extension advises against overhead watering and watering at night for basil, to lower the risk of downy mildew.

UAE tap water is desalinated and then remineralised, and its mineral content varies by area and building. Clemson Extension says white to grey crusty deposits on the soil or the pot rim are a sign of salt build-up: drench the pot with plenty of water to wash the salts out, or repot into fresh potting mix.
tips: Never leave a tulsi pot standing in water. Wet roots are a bigger risk than a pot that dries out once.

care_sections.heading: What soil and pot does tulsi need?
paragraphs: Tulsi needs a well-drained potting mix in a pot with a drainage hole. NC State Extension says holy basil tolerates a wide range of soil types and pH, but does poorly in waterlogged soil, so drainage matters more than the exact mix.

Tulsi grows well in a pot. Iowa State Extension says basil is well suited to containers, and NC State Extension advises growing holy basil in a container or a confined area, because it seeds itself easily and can become a weed outside its native range.
Move tulsi to a bigger pot when the roots fill the pot or the soil dries out very quickly after watering. In the UAE, most planting and repotting is done in the cooler months, from October to April.
steps: Choose a pot with a drainage hole, a little bigger than the root ball.
Put fresh, well-drained potting mix in the bottom of the new pot.
Take the tulsi out of its old pot and set it at the same depth as before.
Fill around the roots with potting mix and press it down lightly.
Water thoroughly until water runs out of the hole, then empty the saucer.

care_sections.heading: How do you prune tulsi, slow its flowering and harvest the leaves?
paragraphs: Prune a tulsi plant by cutting or pinching the stem tips regularly, which keeps it bushy and slows flowering. Iowa State Extension says removing basil stem tips makes the plant branch and extends the harvest, and UT Gardens notes that tulsi can be cut several times through the summer and grows back from the stem joints.

Tulsi flowers in spikes of tiny white, pale pink or lavender flowers (NC State Extension). If you grow tulsi for its leaves, pick them before the flowers open: Iowa State Extension says basil has the most flavour when the flower buds have formed but before they open, and that much of the leaf flavour fades once seed forms.

Penn State Extension advises pinching out the growing tips of basil to slow flowering and promote leafy growth. If you want tulsi seeds, or the bees that visit the flowers (UT Gardens), let some spikes flower.
In Hindu households tulsi is sacred, and UT Gardens notes that it is common to ask permission from the plant before harvesting.
steps: Use clean scissors or your fingers.
Cut each stem just above a pair of leaves. New shoots grow from that joint.
Pinch out the growing tips often to slow flowering.
Use the leaves straight away, or keep the cut stems in the fridge (Penn State Extension).

care_sections.heading: Does tulsi need fertiliser?
paragraphs: Tulsi needs only light feeding while it is growing. Use a balanced or organic plant food at the strength on the label. Do not overdo nitrogen: Iowa State Extension says too much nitrogen affects the flavour of basil.
In the UAE, tulsi grows most actively in the warm months, and growth slows in winter. Feed while it is putting out new shoots, and stop when growth slows.

care_sections.heading: How do you grow tulsi from seed?
paragraphs: Grow tulsi from seed by sowing it thinly in moist seed or potting mix, in a warm place, with bright light for the seedlings. Iowa State Extension says basil seeds germinate best at about 24 °C (75 °F), and that seedlings need bright light so they do not become leggy. NC State Extension notes that tulsi also seeds itself.
In the UAE, sow tulsi seeds in the cooler months, from October to April. In the summer heat, sow indoors in a bright spot instead.
steps: Fill a small pot or seed tray with moist seed or potting mix.
Keep the mix damp and warm, and keep the seedlings in bright light so they do not get lanky.
Move the seedlings to their own pots when they are big enough to handle.
Then move the young plants into full sun.

care_sections.heading: Can a tulsi plant grow indoors in the UAE?
paragraphs: A tulsi plant can grow indoors in the UAE only at the sunniest window you have, with direct sun for most of the day, and it grows best outdoors. Iowa State Extension notes that basil grown indoors has a less intense flavour and fragrance.

In an AC room away from a window, tulsi gets too little light: the growth gets weak and spindly, the leaves get pale, and the plant slowly declines. Many UAE towers also have tinted glass, which reduces the light indoors. If your tulsi has to live inside, put it right next to the brightest window.

first_week.intro: A new tulsi plant needs sun and an eye on the soil in its first week. The main risks are a dry pot in the heat and a dark spot indoors.
steps: Put the tulsi in its sunniest spot: a balcony, terrace, garden or the brightest window. From May to September, choose a spot with afternoon shade.
Feel the soil on the day it arrives, and water if the top is dry. Small nursery pots dry out fast in the heat.
Check that water runs out of the drainage hole, and empty the saucer.
Do not repot straight away. Let the plant settle in its pot first, and repot when the roots fill it.

uae_year.care: Tulsi copes with heat, but give the pot morning sun and afternoon shade. Small pots dry fastest: test the soil more often in heatwaves and water at the base, early in the day. Pinch out the stem tips to slow flowering.
The best time to sow tulsi seeds, repot, and move plants back into full sun. Growth is strong: cut the tips often to keep the plant bushy, and feed lightly.

Tulsi growth slows and the soil takes longer to dry, so water less and stop feeding. Full sun all day is fine. Coastal winter nights are mild. Inland (Al Ain, desert areas) and in Riyadh or Kuwait, nights can get cold, and basil does not tolerate cold: move pots to a sheltered spot or indoors to a sunny window on cold nights. Make sure outdoor pots drain after rain.
Tulsi grows fast again: feed lightly, cut the tips often and sow new plants from seed. Before May, move pots to a spot with afternoon shade.

problems.question: Why is my tulsi plant drying out and drooping in the heat?
problems.symptom: Drooping stems, dry or crisp leaves in summer
problems.cause: Dry soil in a hot, sunny pot
problems.answer: A tulsi that droops and gets dry, crisp leaves in summer is usually short of water. In the UAE heat, a small pot in full sun can dry out completely between waterings, and the roots cannot keep up.
problems.signs: Soil dry and pulling away from the side of the pot, wilted leaves with brown, crisp edges.
fix: Water the soil thoroughly at the base until water runs out of the drainage hole.
If the soil has shrunk away from the pot, water it a second time (the Clemson Extension double watering method) so the whole root ball gets wet.
Move the pot to a spot with afternoon shade for the rest of the summer.
Test the soil more often in heatwaves, and move the plant to a bigger pot if it dries out very fast.

problems.question: Why are my tulsi leaves turning yellow while the soil stays wet?
problems.answer: Yellow tulsi leaves with soil that stays wet usually mean waterlogged soil. Holy basil does poorly in waterlogged soil (NC State Extension), and Clemson Extension says roots that sit in water cannot take up oxygen and may rot.
problems.signs: Soil still wet long after watering, water in the saucer or cover pot, old and new leaves yellow and drop at the same time (RHS).
fix: Stop watering until the top of the soil feels dry.
Empty the saucer or cover pot, and check that the drainage hole is not blocked.
If the soil stays soggy, repot into fresh, well-drained potting mix in a pot with a drainage hole.
Remove the yellow leaves.
From now on, feel the soil before every watering.

problems.question: Why is my tulsi tall and leggy with few leaves?
problems.symptom: Long, thin stems with few, small leaves
problems.cause: Too little sun, or stems not cut back
problems.answer: A leggy tulsi is usually short of light. Holy basil needs full sun, and in a dim spot or an AC room the stems stretch towards the light. Tulsi that is never cut back also grows tall and sparse.
problems.signs: Long gaps between leaf pairs, weak and spindly stems, pale new leaves.
fix: Move the plant to a spot with six or more hours of direct sun, gradually if it has been in shade.
Cut the long stems back to just above a pair of leaves.
Pinch the stem tips regularly so the plant branches.

problems.question: Why are there tiny white flies and sticky leaves on my tulsi?
problems.symptom: Tiny white flying insects, sticky leaves
problems.answer: Tiny white insects that fly up when you touch a tulsi plant are usually whiteflies. Colorado State University Extension describes them as gnat-like and covered in fine white wax; they suck sap and leave sticky honeydew, and heavily infested plants can drop leaves. Aphids also leave sticky honeydew.
problems.signs: White insects under the leaves that fly up when disturbed, sticky or shiny leaves, weak new growth.
fix: Check the undersides of the leaves.
Hose aphids off with a strong jet of water, as Colorado State University Extension advises.
Hang a yellow sticky card near the plant to trap adult whiteflies.

If whiteflies come back, spray a neem insecticide or insecticidal soap on the undersides of the leaves, as the label says: CSU Extension says these may control the young whiteflies (nymphs) on the leaves.
If you use the leaves, follow the label on how long to wait before you pick them.

problems.question: Why is my tulsi losing leaves in winter?
problems.symptom: Damaged or falling leaves after cold nights
problems.answer: A tulsi that loses leaves in winter has usually had cold nights. Basil does not tolerate cold temperatures and is damaged by frost (Iowa State Extension). Coastal UAE winters are mild, but inland and in colder GCC cities, nights can get cold enough to damage it.
problems.signs: Leaf damage or leaf loss that starts after a cold night.
fix: Move the pot to a sheltered spot against a wall, or indoors to a sunny window, on cold nights.
Water less, because the soil dries more slowly in winter.
Wait for warmer weather, then cut back the damaged stems to just above healthy leaves.

problems.question: Why is my tulsi flowering so much and making fewer leaves?
problems.symptom: Many flower spikes, fewer new leaves
problems.answer: Tulsi flowers a lot because it is an annual or short-lived perennial that sets seed readily. Flowering is normal, but once seed forms, much of the leaf flavour fades (Iowa State Extension, for basil).
problems.signs: Spikes of tiny flowers at most stem tips, then brown seed heads.
fix: Pinch out the growing tips often: Penn State Extension says this slows flowering and promotes branching and leafy growth.
Pick leaves regularly before the flowers form, and cut the stems just above a pair of leaves (Utah State University Extension).
Let a few spikes flower and set seed if you want new plants.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping tulsi in a dim AC room
mistakes.instead: Give it six or more hours of direct sun: a balcony, terrace, garden or the sunniest window.
Feel the top of the soil before each watering. Water when it is dry, and wait when it is damp.

mistakes.mistake: A pot without a drainage hole, or a saucer full of water
mistakes.instead: Use a pot with a drainage hole and empty the saucer after watering. Holy basil does poorly in waterlogged soil.

mistakes.mistake: A small pot in full afternoon sun in the UAE summer
mistakes.instead: Give the pot afternoon shade from May to September, and move the plant to a bigger pot if it dries out very fast.

mistakes.mistake: Letting every stem flower and set seed
mistakes.instead: Pinch out the stem tips often, and pick the leaves before the flowers open.

mistakes.mistake: Feeding heavily with a high-nitrogen fertiliser
mistakes.instead: Feed lightly while it grows. Too much nitrogen affects the flavour of basil.

myths.myth: Tulsi is a houseplant that grows well in any room.
myths.fact: Tulsi needs full sun, six or more hours of direct sun a day. It grows best outdoors in the UAE, or at the sunniest window.

myths.myth: Tulsi and sweet basil are the same plant.
myths.fact: They are two species in the same genus: tulsi is Ocimum tenuiflorum and sweet basil is Ocimum basilicum. Tulsi has hairy stems, fuzzier leaves and a spicy, clove-like scent.

myths.myth: Tulsi needs water every day in summer.
myths.fact: How often tulsi needs water depends on the pot, the sun and the weather. Feel the soil first: water when the top is dry.

pet_safety.summary: No pet-safety listing exists for holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum): the ASPCA plant lists for cats and dogs do not include it. The ASPCA lists sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum), a different species, as non-toxic to cats and dogs, but that listing does not cover tulsi. Keep pets from chewing the plant, and ask your vet if you are unsure.
pet_safety.emergency: If your pet chews or eats tulsi and vomits, has diarrhoea or seems unwell, call your vet or a 24-hour animal emergency clinic and tell them the plant name: holy basil, Ocimum tenuiflorum.

alternatives.name: Sweet Basil
alternatives.light: Full sun; copes with part shade
alternatives.pets: ASPCA: non-toxic to cats and dogs
alternatives.why: You want basil mainly for cooking

alternatives.name: Mint
alternatives.water: Moist soil; does not do well in dry soil
alternatives.pets: ASPCA: toxic to cats and dogs
alternatives.why: You have less sun and want a fast-spreading herb for a pot

alternatives.name: Rosemary
alternatives.water: Dry to medium soil; overwatering is the common cause of decline
alternatives.pets: ASPCA: non-toxic to cats and dogs
alternatives.why: You want a woody, evergreen herb that copes with drought and salt

faqs.q: What is the difference between Rama and Krishna tulsi?
faqs.a: Rama, Krishna and Vana are the three tulsi types named by UT Gardens. Krishna tulsi is the dark, purple type (Cohen, 2014). Rama tulsi has light purple flowers and is the type most common in North American gardens (UT Gardens). Vana tulsi is the white, wild type (Cohen, 2014).

In Hinduism, tulsi is worshipped as a goddess and every part of the plant is considered sacred. Many Hindu households keep a tulsi plant, often in an ornate earthen pot in a courtyard (Cohen, 2014). UT Gardens notes that prayers can begin with an offering of tulsi leaves, and that it is common to ask permission from the plant before harvesting.

faqs.q: Can a tulsi plant stay outside in the UAE summer?
faqs.a: Yes, a tulsi plant can stay outside in the UAE summer, because it likes heat. Give it morning sun and afternoon shade, and test the soil more often in heatwaves, because small pots dry out fast. A bigger pot holds water for longer than a small one.

faqs.q: What is the difference between tulsi and sweet basil?
faqs.a: Tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum) and sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum) are two species of basil. Tulsi has hairy green or purple stems, fuzzier and often purple-tinged leaves, smaller flowers and a spicy flavour of clove, mint and basil. Both need full sun and moist, well-drained soil.

faqs.q: Can tulsi grow in the shade?
faqs.a: Tulsi does not grow well in the shade. Holy basil needs full sun, six or more hours of direct sun a day, and in shade it gets leggy with few leaves. In the UAE summer, afternoon shade is helpful, but the plant still needs direct sun for the rest of the day.

faqs.q: How long does a tulsi plant live?
faqs.a: A tulsi plant is an annual or short-lived perennial (NC State Extension), so it does not live for many years like a shrub. Tulsi seeds itself easily, so you can keep new plants coming from its seeds.

Yes, tulsi is a culinary herb. NC State Extension says it is used in Asian cooking in the same ways as sweet basil, usually cooked or steeped as a tea rather than eaten raw. Iowa State Extension notes its use in some Thai cooking.

faqs.q: Does tulsi spread on its own?
faqs.a: Yes, tulsi seeds itself easily, and new seedlings can come up around the plant. NC State Extension notes that holy basil can be an aggressive weed outside its native range and advises growing it in a container or a confined area.
